summary.value: The authors adapt a DAgger-like algorithm to LM agent fine-training. The authors raised several concerns, notably the limited novelty of the algorithm (in the context of existing DAgger-like algorithms), the implementation using uniform sampling, how to choose the BC vs OEC data ratio, comparison with RL using verifiable rewards, or the under-exploitation of the expert portion data.

reviewer_concerns.value:
Following the reviews, the authors adjusted the claim about their proposition as the first adaptation of a DAgger-like algorithm to LM agent training, which is also used to explain the simplicity of its implementation based on uniform sampling. However, I think using an expert to complete a trajectory generated by the student model is quite straightforward, which is actually also used in Agent-RLVR for instance (although not in the BC setting). The authors ran new experiments to compare with Agent-RLVR in the low data regime (2000 samples). However, I believe in this regime, BC-based algorithms would naturally outperform RL-based algorithms. 
In addition, the authors do not provide responses about some points raised by the reviewers. For instance, why does increasing OEC data may hurt the performance? Or the expert portion data could be further exploited during training (e.g., export portion > student-generated portion).

reviewer_scores.value: It's not clear to me that the reviewers would increase significantly their scores.

comment.value:
Thank you for your review. We are glad you find our experiments convincing to support the claim that we “*outperform the baselines in both 7B and 32B settings*” on SWE-bench and see the strength that OEC is “*compatible with any combination of student and expert*”. We invite you to read the global rebuttal that discusses **new experiment results** we’ve run to compare OECs against an RL baseline along with a new detailed comparison of the computation complexity between OEC and traditional DAgger. We address each of your individual concerns as follows:

> 1. Switching to the LLM expert at a random step is an inefficient and outdated way to collect online correction data. A better method is to let the expert take over when the student is about to make a mistake, such as LEAP [1], or analyze a complete failure rollout to identify the error steps and provide feedback, such as LFM [2].

Since our paper is **the first application of a DAgger-based approach to LM agent training**, we wanted to keep our experimentation and methodology simple. However, one of the strengths of the OEC framework is that it enables switching from student to expert at any timestep based on a variety of methods. We’re excited to see future work to experiment with more sophisticated methods.

> 2. Apart from the corrective actions, LLM experts can also provide reward signals and trajectory preference pairs. Agent-RLVR [3] uses the expert to generate a corrected trajectory t' for a failed rollout t and performs preference learning over (t, t'), instead of doing behavioral cloning on t'. IRPO [4] and DMPO [5] use LLM-provided reward models to finetune the student via preference learning. In contrast, OEC discards the student's portion and only performs training on the expert portion of each trajectory, which may have lower training efficiency.

In fact, our ablations found the opposite to be true! Table 2 in the paper shows an ablation that we performed that shows that discarding the student’s portion of the trajectory actually improves performance (absolute +6% in 7B and +3.6% in 32B).

> 3. The baselines are insufficient. In the paper, OEC is only compared against behavioral cloning and on-policy trajectories. Several prior works [1–5] share a similar teacher-student-learning setting (especially [3]), but the paper does not demonstrate that OEC achieves better sample efficiency or faster training compared to them.

Inspired by your comment, we ran a **new baseline experiment against Agent-RLVR [3]** that shows that **OEC outperforms this RL-based method**. Please see the global rebuttal for details that will be included in the final version of the paper. Thank you for your suggestions since we feel this significantly strengthens our results and claims.

> 4. The OEC algorithm is essentially a variant of DAgger with limited novelty. DAgger (S Ross et al. 2010) has a lot of variants in robotics and RL, including EnsembleDAgger (K Menda et al. 2018), ThriftyDAgger (R Hoque et al. 2021), etc. These variants involve expert interventions in a much more interactive way, allowing the expert to take over when the agent is uncertain or is about to fail. OEC's sample complexity may be reduced if it uses these DAgger-variants to collect correction trajectories.

Since our paper is the first application of a DAgger-based approach to LM agent training, we wanted to keep our experimentation and methodology simple. We primarily focused on adapting traditional DAgger to the LM agent domain and came up with OECs that reduce the computational complexity of DAgger from an O(T^2) dependency to O(T) with OECs (where T is the number of timesteps). This dependency makes DAgger prohibitive to run in the LM agent setting. See the global rebuttal for more details of this new analysis that we will include in the final version of the paper. 

## Questions:

> 1. Can OEC be deployed to other tasks? Does OEC still outperform baselines in the tasks other than SWE-bench? Why does the paper choose this task?

OEC is very flexible and can easily be deployed to generate training data in other tasks. We expect OEC to provide the biggest gains in long horizon tasks that are at risk of the most covariate shift. We focus on SWE tasks because they provide a setting with some of the longest horizon tasks currently being performed by LM agents and also allow verification via unit tests. We will further clarify this motivation for the final version.

> 2. Can you further explain the "on-policy" baseline? When the trajectories are entirely rolled out by the student model, how do you use the expert model for supervised fine-tuning?

The expert model is not used for the “on-policy” baseline. This method rolls out trajectories using the student model (so that the trajectories are entirely on-policy), uses rejection sampling to filter out failed trajectories, and then performs SFT on the remaining successful samples.

summary.value: The paper introduces a method, termed `on-policy expert corrections (OECs)`, to improve imitation learning (i.e., finetuning on expert trajectories) for LLMs. The main problem they are trying to address is covariate shift in standard behavior cloning. OEC is a data-collection scheme where on-policy data from the learner is collected till a random timestep for each trajectory, and then the expert policy is used to collect data for the rest of the trajectory. They conduct experiments on SWE tasks, and show that a combination of standard behavior cloning and learning from OEC data improves over standard behavior cloning alone.

strengths.value:
The paper identifies an important that hasn’t been addressed yet (covariate shift in behavior cloning for LLMs), and proposes a well-motivated and easy-to-understand method

The experiment design is appropriate for the claims in the paper, and there’s evidence that (i) there is covariate shift between learner and expert’s policies trajectory distribution, and (ii) OECs improve performance for SWE task for 7B and 32B models derived from Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct series. They include additional experiments (i) showing that masking loss from the learner’s part of the trajectory and filtering out repetitive trajectories is important for good performance, and (ii) showing a LLM-as-a-judge analysis of failure modes of the models trained with different strategies, which is great to have.

The presentation is very clear.

weaknesses.value:
The paper introduces OEC as a novel data-generation method, but this strategy of learning from trajectories where we use on-policy behavior till a certain timestep and then switching to expert policy for the rest of the episode has been studied before. For example, this family of strategies is the focus of “Learning to Search Better than Your Teacher” by Chang et. al. at ICML 2015. I think the paper should cite and discuss previous work on OEC in the related works section, and appropriately frame its contribution (e.g., bringing this idea to the setting of behavior cloning for LLMs).

A significant issue with the experiments is that they are performed with a single seed, so there are no error bars. There is past work showing there is significant variation in LLM performance across fine-tuning runs [1, 2, 3], which makes the results suspect. I understand that single-seed results are somewhat the norm in the field due to computational costs, I think the paper should at least acknowledge this limitation.

1. Assessing the Macro and Micro Effects of Random Seeds on Fine-Tuning Large Language Models by Zhou, Savova and Wang
2. Measuring the Instability of Fine-Tuning by Du and Nguyen
3. On the Stability of Fine-tuning BERT: Misconceptions, Explanations, and Strong Baselines by Mosbach, Andriushchenko and Klakow

Finally, it seems like the best results in the experiments are obtained by a combination of behavior-cloning using expert data and OEC data, but the paper doesn’t suggest a strategy for choosing the ratio of both data sources. Looking at Figure 3, it seems like including a small amount of OEC data could even degrade performance sometimes.

summary.value:
The paper introduces an approach to finetune existing LLMs with on-policy expert corrections. The idea is to use a combination of on-policy and expert samples to construct trajectories, and only update the model with the expert portion of the trajectory. This helps mitigate the effect of covariate shift but also stabilizes training with on-policy samples. Experiments are conducted in software engineering tasks with improvements over prior works.

The method is a simple variation of online imitation learning, and shows good empirical results. Analysis on the covariate shift between student and expert policies offers an interesting view of the problem.

* Emperical results show improvements over prior works on open benchmark
* The analysis on covariate shift is nicely done

Thank you for your review. We are glad you found the “*idea of the approach is simple and easy to follow*” and that the “*analysis on covariate shift is nicely done*”. We invite you to read the global rebuttal that discusses **new experimental results** we’ve run to compare OECs against an RL baseline along with a new detailed comparison of the computation complexity between OEC and traditional DAgger. We address each of your individual concerns as follows:

## Weaknesses:

> The author mentions the potential of using RL with verifier rewards, but does not compare with any baselines using RL.

In response to your review, we have **run new experiments against a recent RL method** in the SWE-agent domain that uses verified rewards. Our method outperforms this new baseline and we feel it greatly strengthens our results, indicating that OECs can show improvement over traditional imitation learning *and RL*. Please see the global rebuttal for further details.

> Based on results, later switching improves the model more, but the method uses uniform sampling to determine the switch time. This seems to be a bit contradictory.

We primarily chose a uniform distribution for simplicity and straightforward experimentation. This sampling strategy also allowed us to easily reuse the samples to perform the “switch time” ablation to study its impact. We don’t claim that uniform sampling is the best strategy and see the flexibility to easily implement new sampling strategies as one of OEC’s strengths. We are excited to see more sophisticated sampling strategies developed in future work.

> There are no explanations on the results provided in Table 3, so I am a bit confused about the meaning of this experiment.

This figure is discussed in the paragraph in the middle of page 7 beginning with “A combination of OEC and BC trajectories performs best.“ This experiment explores the performance impact on altering the mixture between traditional BC and OEC trajectories, demonstrating that a mixture of the trajectory types outperforms each individually.

> Minor issue with y-axis on figure 2(a), showing 0.17% resolution rate (I believe that it is a plotting mistake?)

Thank you for catching this mistake, it will be fixed in the final version.

## Questions:

> What is the rejection sampling with supervised finetuning procedure? Is it simply using successful trajectories from the verifier for supervised training?

Yes, that is correct. We will further clarify this in section 3.2. This training scheme is used across all algorithms and baselines.

> What is the reasoning behind sampling from uniform distribution as opposed to other distributions, e.g. geometric distribution? Given that experiment results show that switching later is better?

Mainly for simplicity and easy experimentation. See above for more details.

> How does the method work compared to DAgger?

An exact DAgger-like algorithm is too computationally expensive to run in our setting (it requires an O(T^2) dependency where T is the number of steps as opposed to the O(T) dependency enjoyed by OEC). See the global response for a new detailed analysis between the approaches that we will add to the final version.

> What does finetuning the student model from scratch mean? Do you initialize the weights to be random?

No, we initialize the weights to the pretrained LLM student (based on the Qwen2.5-Coder family). The same student is used across algorithms and baselines. We have clarified this for the final version.

> Why is BC data added only to the 32B setting and not the 7B setting? Why is BC data important in one setting and not the other?

BC data is added to the 7B setting as well: a flat 1000 samples across all experiments. These additional samples are counted in the x-axis value. We will clarify this point in the final version in the caption of Figure 2 and Section 4.2.

> Are there any theoretical guarantees in terms of regret bounds for this algorithm?

OEC trajectories are similar to learning-to-search methods (e.g., “Learning to Search Better than Your Teacher” by Chang et. al. at ICML 2015) that have no-regret guarantees so we hope some guarantees can be established in followup work.

We thank all of the reviewers for their helpful feedback and for improving the paper. In response to reviewer feedback, we have made the following changes to the paper:
- We ran a **new experiment against a recent RL baseline** that shows that OEC achieves substantial gains. This extends our experimental results to demonstrate that OECs also show substantial improvement over an RL method. See below for details. 
- We added a **new complexity comparison between traditional DAgger and OECs** that highlights the computation complexity limitations of DAgger which makes it impractical to apply to our long-horizon LM agent setting. See below for details.
- Clarified our contributions to reflect that OECs are the **first extension of existing DAgger-based approaches to a LM agent setting** while being based on existing DAgger-based methods.
- Added a better comparison to several existing works (e.g., (Ross & Bagnell, 2014) and (Chang et. al., 2015)).
- More precisely defined the class in which our results are SOTA.
- Better communicated the results in Fig 3 and included suggestions for selecting the ratio between OEC and BC data.
- Included a more thorough discussion of the limitations imposed by single-seed experiments.
- Clarified additional points about reinitializing weights, problem instances, the rejection sampling procedure, training data mixtures, ablation results, and the on-policy baseline.

Finally, we wanted to thank the reviewers for identifying the main strengths of the paper: (1) OECs being the first extension of DAgger-based methods to LM agent training, (2) motivating the approach through experiments that quantify turn-wise divergence between student and expert, and (3) experiments that show that OEC consistently outperforms existing approaches.

## New experiments comparing OEC against an RL baseline

In response to suggestions by several reviewers, we have run initial experiments against a new recent RL approach for finetuning LM agents in the SWE agent domain. As explicitly suggested by Reviewer CGxJ, we chose Agent-RLVR [1], a recent RL-based method for training LM agents in the SWE agent domain, for this comparison. So far we have tested Agent-RLVR under the same conditions presented in Figure 2a in the paper: the 7B student with rollouts on the same problem distribution and 2000 training samples. The eval results on SWE-bench Lite are presented in the following table and show that OEC achieves similar performance gains over Agent-RLVR:


| Number of Samples | OEC (ours) | Agent-RLVR (new) | On-policy | BC    |
| ----------------- | ---------- | ---------- | --------- | ----- |
| 2000              | **14.7%**    | 13.7%      | 13.7%     | 13.7% |


Our results indicate that Agent-RLVR achieves similar performance as BC and on-policy in the 7B setting resulting in a substantial increase when using OEC. We will run experiments at the remaining data scales (3000 and 4000) and include the results in the final version of the paper. We thank the reviewers for this suggestion since we believe a direct comparison against an RL-based method greatly strengthens the results and claims of the paper, demonstrating the OECs shows improvement over both traditional imitation learning *and RL*.

[1] Agent-RLVR: Training Software Engineering Agents via Guidance and Environment Rewards, J Da et al. 2025.


## New complexity comparison between traditional DAgger and OECs in the LM agent setting

One of the major reasons DAgger requires adaptation in the LM agent setting is that traditional **DAgger-style algorithms have an O(T^2) (where T is the number of turns) dependency to generate expert rollouts and train the student in comparison to the O(T) dependency that OEC enjoys**. DAgger incurs an O(T^2) dependency in the LM setting because it cannot reuse the KV cache from previous calls to the expert throughout a trajectory. The KV cache needs to be recomputed for every single call to the expert since the expert's generations are different from the student' trajectory. The exact same issue occurs during training time, not allowing us to take advantage of efficient KV caching as is done with traditional LLM training. On the other hand, the KV cache in an OEC trajectory only needs to be recomputed a single-time, when switching from the student to the expert, and following turns can incrementally add to the KV cache. This applies during expert generation and training resulting in OECs being a much more efficient approach when applied to LM agent training. This discussion will be included and highlighted in the final version of the paper.

Thank you for your review. We appreciate your recognition that the paper successfully “*motivat[es] partial on-policy corrections*” and that the experiments show that OEC “*yields consistent gains over BC and fully on-policy data*”. We invite you to read the global rebuttal that discusses **new experiment results** we’ve run to compare OECs against an RL baseline along with a new detailed comparison of the computation complexity between OEC and traditional DAgger. We address each of your individual concerns as follows:

> 1. Limited novelty relative to established interactive IL.

There is certainly a strong overlap between OEC and existing DAgger-style algorithms; our primary contribution is in adapting these algorithms so that they can be successfully applied to an LM agent domain along with a suite of experiments that demonstrate its success. As far as we can tell, our paper is **the first to explore extending DAgger style algorithms to LM agent training**. We will further emphasize our core contribution and the distinction from existing work in the introduction of the paper and in discussion of related works. Here is a paragraph that we are planning to add to the related works:

*DAgger has spawned many followup works since its introduction. Most close to our approach are methods  (Ross & Bagnell, 2014) and (Chang et. al., 2015) that “roll-in” with a student policy and then “roll-out” with an expert model to compute single-step cost-to-go values used for policy improvement. Our method instead uses the expert portion of the rollout directly for imitation learning, allowing it to be applied to training LM agents (where updating policies using cost-to-go values is impractical) via straightforward supervised fine-tuning.*

One of the major reasons DAgger requires adaptation in the LM agent setting is that traditional DAgger-style algorithms in the LM agent setting have an O(T^2) (where T is the number of turns) dependency to generate expert rollouts and train the student in comparison to the O(T) dependency that OEC enjoys. We mention this in the final paragraph of page 3.1 but will include a much more thorough analysis in the final version. Please see the global rebuttal for a draft of this analysis.

> 2. SOTA framing is ambiguous.

All of our experiments were rigorously conducted to make sure that all algorithms (including baseline and ablations) are subject to an equitable comparison. All algorithms use the same LM student model backbone (Qwen-2.5-Coder family), verifier usage (based on test cases), and the same inference-time scaling (pass@1, 75 steps). Additionally, they all use the same problem instance training distribution, positive training set size, and SFT implementation and parameters for finetuning. Within this class, OEC consistently outperforms baselines and achieves SOTA on SWE-bench across existing imitation learning approaches in the 7b and 32b setting. We’ve even run new experiments in a RL baseline for more direct comparison to other methods (see the global review for details) that show similar improvement. We will further clarify all of these points in the results section in the introduction and the experiments.

> 3. Possible confounds from distribution differences.

All algorithms and baselines are subject to the same training data distribution. The only exception is a single datapoint in Figure 2b that uses additionally collected problem instances to further scale the number of OEC training samples. This datapoint is clearly marked with a dashed line and we explain in the text how these additional problem instances are sourced. Even without this extra datapoint, OEC strongly outperforms the baselines.

summary.value: The paper introduces On-Policy Expert Corrections for LLMs' imitation learning, collecting expert correction data by rolling out student trajectories and switching to the expert midway. This allows training on on-policy states while involving expert supervision. Experiments on software engineering tasks show that OECs outperform both behavioral cloning and learning on fully on-policy data.

strengths.value:
1. The experiment is performed on the newly released SWE-bench benchmark, outperforming the baselines in both 7B and 32B settings.
2. The OEC framework is compatible with any combination of student and expert language models.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Switching to the LLM expert at a random step is an inefficient and outdated way** to collect online correction data. A better method is to let the expert take over when the student is about to make a mistake, such as LEAP [1], or analyze a complete failure rollout to identify the error steps and provide feedback, such as LFM [2].  

2. Apart from the corrective actions, **LLM experts can also provide reward signals and trajectory preference pairs**. Agent-RLVR [3] uses the expert to generate a corrected trajectory t' for a failed rollout t and performs preference learning over (t, t'), instead of doing behavioral cloning on t'. IRPO [4] and DMPO [5] use LLM-provided reward models to finetune the student via preference learning. In contrast, **OEC discards the student's portion and only performs training on the expert portion of each trajectory**, which may have lower training efficiency.  

3. The baselines are insufficient. In the paper, OEC is **only compared against behavioral cloning and on-policy trajectories**. Several prior works [1–5] share a similar teacher-student-learning setting (especially [3]), but the paper does not demonstrate that OEC achieves better sample efficiency or faster training compared to them.

4. The OEC algorithm is **essentially a variant of DAgger with limited novelty**. DAgger (S Ross et al. 2010) has a lot of variants in robotics and RL, including EnsembleDAgger (K Menda et al. 2018), ThriftyDAgger (R Hoque et al. 2021), etc. These variants involve expert interventions in a much more interactive way, allowing the expert to take over when the agent is uncertain or is about to fail. OEC's sample complexity may be reduced if it uses these DAgger-variants to collect correction trajectories.

References:  
[1] Better than Your Teacher: LLM Agents that learn from Privileged AI Feedback, S Choudhury et al. 2024  
[2] Policy Improvement using Language Feedback Models, V Zhong et al. 2024  
[3] Agent-RLVR: Training Software Engineering Agents via Guidance and Environment Rewards, J Da et al. 2025  
[4] Iterative Reasoning Preference Optimization, RY Pang et al. 2024  
[5] Direct Multi-Turn Preference Optimization for Language Agents, W Shi et al. 2024

questions.value:
1. Can OEC be deployed to other tasks? Does OEC still outperform baselines in the tasks other than SWE-bench? Why does the paper choose this task?
2. Can you further explain the "on-policy" baseline? When the trajectories are entirely rolled out by the student model, how do you use the expert model for supervised fine-tuning?

summary.value: The paper tackles covariate shift for multi-turn LM agents on SWE-bench, proposing On-policy Expert Corrections (OEC): roll out the student on-policy, switch to an expert model at a randomly sampled turn, keep only the expert segment (student tokens are masked during SFT), and filter trajectories via unit-test verification and simple repetition heuristics. Claimed contributions are: (i) an analysis showing student–expert divergence grows with depth; (ii) the OEC data-generation recipe (random switch + masking + verifier filtering); (iii) improved pass@1 over behavioral cloning (BC) and fully on-policy data under their setup; and (iv) ablations isolating the importance of masking and repetition filtering. Key evidence comes from scaling curves (OEC > BC > on-policy), covariate-shift diagnostics across turns, and controlled ablations on filtering/masking.

strengths.value:
- The paper empirically quantifies turn-wise divergence between student and expert, motivating partial on-policy corrections.

- OEC is simple to implement (random switch, mask student tokens, verifier-gated acceptance) and yields consistent gains over BC and fully on-policy data under the stated setup.

- The study isolates two actionable levers—on-policy masking and repetition filtering—and shows they materially affect results, especially at larger model scales.

- Findings like “later switches help,” and “unit-test filtering alone is insufficient without anti-loop filters,” offer concrete guidance to practitioners training SWE agents.

weaknesses.value:
1. **Limited novelty relative to established interactive IL.**

   **Problem:** OEC’s core idea—on-policy rollouts with expert corrections—substantially overlaps with DAgger-style data aggregation and related learning-to-search methods; the paper’s unique elements are mainly engineering choices (random switch policy and masking) rather than a new principle. ICLR, novelty beyond well-known IL frameworks is expected; otherwise significance hinges on breadth and rigor of validation.

   **Action:** Clearly position OEC against DAgger/LOLS/AggreVaTeD, including a small theoretical or synthetic analysis of the bias introduced by masking/truncation and the effect of the switch-time distribution; add a controlled comparison to a **DAgger-like** baseline adapted to the same scaffold. 

2. **SOTA framing is ambiguous.**

   **Problem:** The paper claims or suggests “SOTA within class,” but the comparison set and constraints (backbone, scaffold, verifier usage, inference-time scaling) are not crisply defined, and some numbers are very close to strong baselines (Table 1). Without a precise protocol, improvements may reflect differences in test-time scaling or data collection rather than the training recipe.
   
   **Action:** Define the comparison “class” explicitly; if SOTA is not supported under strict parity (same scaffold, retries, timeouts, verifier configs), rephrase to “competitive.”


3. **Possible confounds from distribution differences.**

   **Problem:** Some OEC points in scaling plots appear to mix slightly different instance distributions compared to BC/on-policy. The gains could partially come from instance mix rather than the method.

   **Action:** Re-run scaling where all regimes are collected on the same fixed instance set.

questions.value:
1. Please define precisely what “state-of-the-art in their respective classes” means (backbone size, scaffold, verifier rules, retries/timeouts, inference-time scaling). Under those constraints, is OEC actually SOTA?
2. How many evaluation retries, max turns, and unit-test limits were used across methods? Were they identical for all baselines?
3. Can you report mean ± std over ≥3 seeds for all key numbers and curves?
4. What is the instance overlap (if any) among expert demos used for pretraining, OEC/BC/on-policy training data, and evaluation splits?
5. Please provide a controlled comparison to a **DAgger-like baseline** adapted to your scaffold, and discuss how masking/truncation differs theoretically from classic dataset aggregation.
6. Could you release the exact repetition-filtering heuristics (regexes/thresholds) and masking implementation code?
7. Have you tested OEC beyond SWE-bench (e.g., SWE-bench-Live or a non-SWE agent domain)? If not, can you discuss expected limitations?

> 3. Finally, it seems like the best results in the experiments are obtained by a combination of behavior-cloning using expert data and OEC data, but the paper doesn’t suggest a strategy for choosing the ratio of both data sources. Looking at Figure 3, it seems like including a small amount of OEC data could even degrade performance sometimes.

Figure 3 explores scaling the ratio between OEC and BC trajectories. The blue line varies the number of BC trajectories while leaving the OEC samples fixed and the red line varies the number of OEC samples while keeping BC fixed. The results demonstrate the strongest improvement with an equal mix between OEC and BC samples, suggesting this mix as an effective ratio for training. Thus, this is the ratio we use for the experiments in Figure 2b. We will integrate this explanation into the final version of the paper to recommend an equal mix between data types for practitioners.

## Questions

> 1. Please define precisely what “state-of-the-art in their respective classes” means (backbone size, scaffold, verifier rules, retries/timeouts, inference-time scaling). Under those constraints, is OEC actually SOTA?

Yes, OEC is SOTA under these constraints--all constraints are the same across algorithms. See the above response to Weakness 2 for details. We have clarified this for the final version.

> 2. How many evaluation retries, max turns, and unit-test limits were used across methods? Were they identical for all baselines?

They are all identical. We used pass@1 for evaluations, 75 max turns, and used all pass-to-fail unit-tests as is standard for evaluation. We have clarified this for the final version.

> 3. Can you report mean ± std over ≥3 seeds for all key numbers and curves?

We use a temperature of zero for our rollout generation and evaluation so there is no variance from these factors. As Reviewer Wgwf pointed out, the only source of variance is from the SFT training, but we use the standard approach (due to computational limits) of running experiments over a single SFT training run for each datapoint.

> 4. What is the instance overlap (if any) among expert demos used for pretraining, OEC/BC/on-policy training data, and evaluation splits?

Evaluation (on SWE-bench) is entirely separate from training (on SWE-smith). We use the same problem instances across all OEC/BC/on-policy training for fair comparison. We have clarified this for the final version.

> 5. Please provide a controlled comparison to a DAgger-like baseline adapted to your scaffold, and discuss how masking/truncation differs theoretically from classic dataset aggregation.

An exact DAgger-like algorithm is too computationally expensive to run in our setting. See our response to Weakness 1 and the global rebuttal for more details.

> 6. Could you release the exact repetition-filtering heuristics (regexes/thresholds) and masking implementation code?

Yes, we will include this filtering script in the open-source codebase.

>7. Have you tested OEC beyond SWE-bench (e.g., SWE-bench-Live or a non-SWE agent domain)? If not, can you discuss expected limitations?

We have not. We believe that OEC is likely to have the most success over traditional imitation learning in settings where agents are completing long-horizon tasks since this is where we would expect the most covariate shift throughout a rollout. We expect OEC to have a weaker impact on shorter agentic tasks. We will include a more detailed discussion of this point in the limitations section of the final paper.
